summary:
Guainía department lies in Colombia's frontier 'orden público' belt, where armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate day-to-day conduct. That is the operative security context for a trans visitor here. No department-specific legal or enforcement deviation is on record for Guainía, so formal exposure is assessed against the national framework and its enforcement record.

That framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and passports issued within Colombia have offered three gender options (male, female, X) since August 2023. Adults can change legal gender before a notary with a free simultaneous name change on first request.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since the Constitutional Court's 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, and adoption by same-sex couples since November 2015.

Access to premises and to dignified detention rest on court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at a Cali mall) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict; a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

The legal position and the lived position diverge sharply. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video circulated showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was", President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, and reporting counts eight trans women killed between February and April 2024. CNN follow-up reporting of 6 August 2025 found killings of LGBTQ+ people continuing after the Millerey case, with gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns on the street and via WhatsApp announce a "social cleansing" of "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes, 51, was given one week by three armed men to leave town or be killed, hid for a week and then fled at night, having been forced to move twice. In Caquetá and comparable departments, discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, and Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011, giving a formal complaint route that sits alongside the security picture above. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling.

Guainía's position resembles other Colombian border departments where the armed-group pattern has been documented rather than any distinct trans regime: Caquetá and Guajira both show flyer campaigns, threatened displacement and killings attributed to groups still in place after the 2016 peace agreement. Reporting on those departments describes calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, which is the closest available analogue for what a trans visitor in Guainía should expect from non-state actors.

The gap between statute and enforcement is the recurring finding of external review. The UN Human Rights Committee noted concern after the 2023 transitional-justice indictments, and the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission found institutional progress unmatched by daily experience. Formal legal gains therefore do not function as a security guarantee in frontier departments.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on their cédula and other national identification by signing a document before a notary, with a free simultaneous name change on first request, and identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X) since August 2023, and legal gender can be changed without surgery under Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993.

Residents married abroad to a partner of the same sex are registered by notaries and registrars under a National Registry memo issued after the first such registration in March 2016, and hold the same visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers. Same-sex couples have been able to marry since April 2016 and to adopt since November 2015.

Domestic protections on premises and detention include judgments T-314 of 2011, T-909 of 2011 and T-301 of 2004 on access to hotels, malls and public spaces, a 2011 ruling permitting a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a later ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree obliges government institutions on LGBTI rights in education, health care, prisons and as conflict victims, and the May 2018 executive decree extends guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. The 2011 discrimination law gives residents a statutory basis for complaints.

The resident-facing risk is the same one documented in other departments: armed-group kill lists and "social cleansing" campaigns, forced displacement of named trans women, and an economy in which discrimination confines trans women largely to hairdressing or sex work. In Guainía, enforcement of these protections rests with departmental police who do not effectively control the territory.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory supplies no Guainía-specific finding: the departmental entry used here carries no usable content on trans legal status, facilities, enforcement or documented incidents, and the CNN and Guardian items likewise contain no Guainía detail. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework plus the department's classification as a frontier security zone, and any Guainía-specific incident record remains unresolved rather than absent.

Not sourced: whether Guainía's police or prosecutors have recorded any complaint under the 2011 discrimination law, and whether the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree's procedural obligations have been implemented in departmental institutions. No information is available here on facility access, healthcare availability or IDC/information-and-documentation-centre practice within Guainía itself.

Killing totals differ slightly by source and period (more than 40 trans women killed in 2023 in one account, 41 in another; eight between February and April 2024; 13 in the first quarter of 2025; 35 LGBTI murders January to May 2025). The figures are reported for the country as a whole and none can be attributed to Guainía; reconciling them is unresolved.
